Improvement of methane generation capacity by aerobic
pre-treatment of organic waste with a cellulolytic
Trichoderma viride culture
Andreas Otto Wagner*, Thomas Schwarzenauer, Paul Illmer
University of Innsbruck, Institute of Microbiology, Technikerstr. 25, A-6020 Innsbruck, Austria
a r t i c l e i n f o
Article history:
Received 15 April 2013
Received in revised form
23 July 2013
Accepted 25 July 2013
Available online 26 August 2013
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Pre-treatment
Trichoderma viride
Methane
Biogas
a b s t r a c t
Trichoderma viride is known as a potent cellulose decomposer and was successfully used to improve and
accelerate the decomposition process of aerobic composting. In contrast, the role of fungi as pre-
treatment organisms for anaerobic digestion is not clear, since the fast aerobic decomposition is
thought to be responsible for a rapid depletion of easily available nutrients, leading to a lack of these for
the anaerobic community. In the present study carried out in lab-scale, the application of T. viride for the
aerobic pre-incubation of organic matter derived from the inlet port of a 750,000 L anaerobic digester led
to an increase in total gas and methane production in a subsequent anaerobic digestion step. A high
cellulase activity caused by the addition of T. viride seemed to be responsible for a better nutrient
availability for anaerobic microorganisms. Therefore, aerobic pre-incubation of organic residues with T.
viride for subsequent anaerobic digestion is a promising approach in order to increase methane yields.

1. Introduction
Lignocellulose represents a relatively unused source for biogas
(Hendriks and Zeeman, 2009) and consists of three types of poly-
mers e cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin. It represents the major
component of biomass, comprising around half of plant matter
produced by photosynthesis (Perez et al., 2002; Sanchez, 2009).
Many microorganisms are capable of degrading cellulose and using
its breakdown products as a carbon source. Fast degradation of
cellulose mainly takes place in aerobic environments by various
groups of fungi through the production of extracellular cellulolytic
enzymes. In anoxic environments cellulose decomposition is
possible but occurs slowly, requires mixed populations of different
bacteria (Leschine,1995), and often takes place within cellulosomes
(Adney et al., 1991; Desvaux, 2005; Lynd et al., 2002).
Trichoderma viride (Ascomycota, Euascomycetes, Hypocreales,
Hypocreaceae) (de Hoog and Guarro, 1995) is an ubiquitous
saprophytic fungi (Samuels, 1996) widely found in soils and known
to produce cellulases (Lieckfeldt et al., 1999), chitinolytic- (Lorito,
1998), and hemicellulolytic enzymes (Biely and Tenkanen, 1998).
T. viride was successfully used to improve and accelerate the
decomposition of an aerobic composting process (Illmer et al.,
2007). In matrices such as compost, interactions with other or-
ganisms can lead to complete degradation of cellulose (Sanchez,
2009). In contrast, for use as pre-treatment organisms for subse-
quent anaerobic digestion the role of any aerobic fungi is not clear,
since the fast aerobic decomposition might be responsible for a
rapid depletion of easily available nutrients, leading to a lack of
these for a subsequent anaerobic community.
In biogas plants processing waste with high cellulose content
residues, the initial hydrolysis phase is often the process rate-
limiting step, thus hindering the subsequent microbial pop-
ulations producing the desired biogas(es) (Lynd et al., 2002).
Different approaches have been made to enhance both turnover
rates in the hydrolysis phase as well as the extent of hydrolysis in
the anaerobic digestion process by a pre-treatment step. These
include thermal treatment (e.g. Appels et al., 2010), microwave
technology (e.g. Eskicioglu et al., 2007), the direct application of
enzymes (e.g. Gerhardt et al., 2007; Mendes et al., 2006), alkaline
pre-treatment (e.g. Chiu et al., 1997), combined treatments (e.g.
Bougrier et al., 2006) and fungal pre-treatment of fermentation
substrates with selected strains of Sporotrichum, Aspergillus, Fusa-
rium, and Penicillium (e.g. for orange processing waste (Srilatha
et al., 1995)). As far as we know T. viride has not yet been used as
a pre-treatment organism for the improvement of the methane
potential from organic waste designated for anaerobic digestion.

The aim of the present study was to show the beneﬁt of direct
application of T. viride in an aerobic pre-treatment step to enhance
subsequent anaerobic methane production. Measuring cellulase
activity was used to demonstrate the potential of T. viride to
degrade cellulose in organic residue, thus making nutrients avail-
able for the subsequent anaerobic population resulting in an
increased methane production rate.
2. Material and methods
2.1. Cultivation of T. viride
T. viride (Centraalbureau voor Schimmelcultures CBS 456.96)
was cultivated on malt extract agar plates (malt extract 30 g,
peptone 5 g, agar 20 g, 1000 ml distilled water, pH 6.5) at 25 C. For
liquid cultures, a malt extract solution (malt extract 30 g, peptone
5 g, 1000 ml distilled water, pH 6.5) was used, inoculated with a
T. viride from agar plates and cultivated at 25 C at 120 rpm for 3
days. Mycelia were harvested by centrifugation with 5000 g and
washed with 0.9% NaCl solution.
2.2. Aerobic pre-treatment
Bio-waste (Table 1) usually treated in a 900 m3 anaerobic
digestion plant in Roppen, Austria, was used for the aerobic pre-
incubation step. This waste was used to investigate conventional
sludge similar to that often treated in large-scale digestion plants.
An aerobic pre-treatment step was selected since the waste is
usually stored under aerobic conditions for a few days (depending
on the amount of delivered organic waste) without additional
treatment. For a description of running parameters of the digester
and the composition of the sludge refer to Illmer et al. (2009) and
Wagner et al. (2009). Some basic parameters are given in Table 2.
Prior to use, the organic waste was diluted 1:5 with distilled water.
For the aerobic pre-treatment step, 100 g of the diluted waste was
weighted into 250 ml Schott ﬂasks and inoculated with 5.0 g
(variant 5 g) or 15.0 g (variant 15 g) of T. viride fresh weight with a
dry matter content of 5.14% (0.257 g dry matter for the 5 g variant
and 0.771 g dry matter for the 15 g variant). Beside the cellulolytic
potential of T. viride, this organism was selected because of its wide
pH growth range between 1.5 and 9 (de Hoog and Guarro, 1995). As
a control (variant C), diluted waste was used without additional
components. All variants were done in 3 replicates. The ﬂasks were
closed with cotton stoppers and incubated at 25 C for 4 days.
2.3. Anaerobic treatment
After the 4 days of aerobic pre-treatment the samples were
mixed and 10.0 g (0.10 g) were weighted into serum bottles and
ﬂushed with gas consisting of 70% N2 and 30% CO2 for 2 min to
remove headspace oxygen. The bottles were closed with butyl
rubber septa and subsequently inoculated with 5 g of 1:5 diluted
digester outlet sludge (inoculum) to start the anaerobic decompo-
sition process. Additionally 5 g of the anaerobic inoculum were
tested toward methane production from the pure inoculum. All
variants were carried out in triplicate. The ﬂasks were incubated at
52 C for 18 days.
2.4. Experimental design
For the aerobic pre-treatment T. viride was added to diluted
waste and together with not treated controls incubated for 4 days.
Samples for the determination of cellulase activity, organic acids,
glucose concentration, and total carbon and nitrogen were taken at
days 0,1, and 4. Subsequently, the aerobically treated samples (with
and without T. viride application) were used for the anaerobic in-
cubation and inoculated with digester outlet sludge (inoculum)
(anaerobic incubation start ¼ day 0). After inoculation, the ﬂasks
were brought to temperature, the headspace gas concentrations of
H2, CO2 and CH4 were determined by GC measurement, and the
overpressure resulting from the increase in temperature was
removed by a cannula. Overpressure and gas concentration of H2,
CO2, and CH4 in the ﬂasks were measured at days 1, 4, 11, and 18.
Samples for organic acids and glucose determination were taken at
days 0, 1, 4, 11, and 18. The amount of gas production was calculated
from overpressure in the headspace and gas composition.
2.5. Analytical methods
Overpressure in ﬂasks was determined by a pressure measuring
instrument (Greisinger, Germany). Analysis of headspace gas con-
centration of H2, CO2, and CH4 was conducted by GC-analysis using
a Shimadzu GC2010 equipped with a Restek Shin Carbon TS 100/
120 mesh column (length 2 m, 1 mm inner diameter), a wide bore
injector and a thermal conductivity detector as described in
Wagner et al. (2012). Injection volume was 15 ml. For the analysis of
short chain fatty acids (SCFA) via HPLC, a Shimadzu Prominence
System was used with a BioRad AMINEX HPX-87H column, an
isocratic system with 5 mM H2SO4, 65 C, and a ﬂow rate of
0.7 ml min1. Detection was conducted via a UV-detection system
at 210 nm using an external standard (SigmaeAldrich, Germany).
Sample preparation using ﬁltration and centrifugation was carried
out as described previously (Wagner et al., 2010). For glucose
analysis on a Shimadzu Prominence System (HPLC), an aliquot of
the samples used for SCFA analysis was injected (25 ml) onto a
Phenomenex Fast Fruit Column (Phenomenex, Germany) running
with distilled water. For detection, a light scattering detector (LSD)
(Shimadzu) was used, and the calibration was performed by an

2.6. Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using the Software package
Statistica 8.0 (StatSoft Inc., USA).
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Aerobic pre-treatment
Within the 4 days aerobic incubation period transient rates of
cellulase activity could be observed. A signiﬁcant difference
(p < 0.05) was found after 4 days of aerobic incubation between the
variants, indicating a high activity of the added T. viride mycelia. The
highest cellulase activity could be attributed to the 15 g variant,
followed by e and signiﬁcantly different from e the 5 g variant. The
lowest cellulase activity (signiﬁcant p < 0.05) was observed for the
control samples without T. viride inoculation/pre-treatment.
Differences could also be observed in the concentration of
organic acids. The 15 g variant showed distinct and highly signiﬁ-
cant (p < 0.01) differences compared to the other treatments. Be-
side others, butyric and, most notably, acetic acid concentrations in
the 15 g variants were dramatically increased, resulting in a higher
amount of total organic acid concentration (formic-, acetic-, pro-
pionic-, iso-butyric, and butyric acid). The increased acetic acid
concentration (Fig. 1) in particular might have been beneﬁcial for
the subsequent anaerobic treatment, since this organic acid rep-
resents the most important precursor for methane in such envi-
ronments. As a consequence, the high acetate concentration in the
15 g variant also caused an increased acetic:propionic acid ratio
(Ac/Pr ratio) (<10) (data not shown), which is usually thought to be
advantageous for biogas plants. Generally, an Ac/Pr ratio above 2 is
considered as a minimum requirement for stable reactor perfor-
mance, although distinctly lower ratios were also shown to occur
without causing problems as demonstrated by Pullammanappallil
et al. (2001) and Illmer et al. (2009).
For total carbon and total nitrogen, no differences could be
observed during the aerobic incubation step.
3.2. Anaerobic incubation
After 18 days of anaerobic incubation the total gas yield was
signiﬁcantly increased resulting from the aerobic pre-treatment
with T. viride compared to the control without pre-treatment
(Table 3). Most importantly, it was also possible to signiﬁcantly
enhance the methane yield for both T. viride treatments (5 g and
15 g; Table 3, Fig. 2). From all treatments the highest methane

production rates were observed at day 11 of anaerobic incubation,
with the 15 g variant presenting the highest rate. After day 11, the
methane production rate decreased again for all treatments,
although the pre-treated variants still showed a methane produc-
tion (Fig. 2a), whereas the control did not. In comparison to other
treatment methods this yield reﬂects a high methane-forming ef-
ﬁciency. A combined alkaline and ultrasonic treatment (although in
a different matrix and with a different digestion system) led, for
example, to an increase in the methane yield of 150.4 percent (Kim
et al., 2010), whereas an over 400 percent increase was detected in
the present investigation.
The total amount of organic acids, and especially acetic acid,
was signiﬁcantly higher for the 15 g treatment in the ﬁrst days of
anaerobic incubation compared to the control samples, and
decreased after the major part of total methane had been pro-
duced (Fig. 2a). Therefore, a high availability of organic acids
seems to be one of the most important factors for the successful
production of methane. By the application of T. viride for an aer-
obic pre-incubation step this availability was increased signiﬁ-
cantly. Since acetate is the most important precursor of methane,
this might be responsible for the subsequent increase in methane
production.
4. Conclusions
The application of T. viride for the aerobic pre-incubation of
organic matter led to a signiﬁcant and drastic increase in total gas
and methane production in a subsequent anaerobic incubation
step. The measured high cellulase activity caused by the addition of
T. viride seems to be responsible for a better nutrient availability for
anaerobic microorganisms. It could be shown that an aerobic pre-
treatment with T. viride is not responsible for a fast depletion of
nutrients, but instead results in an increase in the available volatile
fatty acid concentration for the subsequent anaerobic microbial
population. Therefore, lab results suggest a high potential for a
large-scale applicability of the proposed pre-treatment method
using T. viride.
